title: Freight broker margins: gross profit vs. take-home income
seoTitle: Freight broker margins: gross profit vs. take-home income
searchIntent: What does a freight broker margin pay for?
excerpt: Understand the shipment spread, the cost of operating a brokerage and why a margin percentage needs context.
takeaway: The difference between the shipper charge and carrier cost is gross profit before the brokerage’s operating expenses. It supports the work of finding, arranging and administering freight; it is not all owner income.

sections.title: Separate shipment spread from take-home income.
paragraphs: Luis’s margin lesson explains that the amount left after paying the carrier is not automatically the owner’s earnings. The brokerage still has work and expenses to support: customer development, communication, administration, technology, staffing, and the handling of problems.

The carrier also operates a business with its own costs. Understanding that perspective makes a rate conversation more useful than assuming that every dollar retained by the other party is unnecessary. Both sides need a service arrangement they can perform.

sections.title: Estimate cost before promising a rate.
paragraphs: The lesson returns to actual carrier requirements rather than an unsupported number offered to win the customer’s attention. Carrier position, preferred destination, truck availability, timing, and lane fit can affect the cost of the move.

Use recent evidence and confirm the service being requested. A historical number may not describe today’s opportunity. If the cost basis is wrong, a seemingly attractive spread can disappear before the shipment is even covered. Pricing discipline begins with understanding what you have committed to arrange.

sections.title: Calculate the shipment margin clearly
paragraphs: For a simple example, charging the customer $2,000 and paying the carrier $1,700 leaves $300 before other costs. That is a 15% gross margin on the $2,000 sale. Markup uses the cost as its denominator, so it is a different calculation.

The example is arithmetic, not a recommended rate. Financing, staff, systems and other costs affect how much remains. A percentage alone cannot tell you whether a particular shipment or brokerage is profitable.

sections.title: Understand the work on both sides
paragraphs: Luis asks brokers and carriers to recognize that each operates a business with real costs. The carrier must understand what it needs to run the truck. The broker must understand the service it is promising and the cost of arranging it.

Use that understanding to negotiate a clear agreement. Quoting a customer without a credible carrier cost can put pressure on everyone later. Know the shipment and confirm the service before committing to the number.

sections.title: Use your own economics instead of a universal target
paragraphs: Costs, service mix, customer payment timing and operating responsibilities differ between brokerages. The margin commentary in the original recording is historical; it should not be treated as a current industry average.

Review actual shipment results and overhead together. Look for work that can be performed reliably at an acceptable return, and understand why a result changed before setting the next price. That is more useful than chasing a percentage detached from the operation.
